## Problem 1

```{r}
ny_noaa
```

The New York NOAA data set measures the precipitation as `prcp`, snow as `snow`, and minimum and maximum temperatures of various New York cities each day. This data set is exceptionally large with dimensions `r ncol(ny_noaa)` by `r nrow(ny_noaa)`. There are multiple entries of missing data with the variables `tmax` and `tmin` completely missing. This becomes an issue without enough information to accurately analyze the data. 


```{r}

ny_noaa_clean =
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na() |>
  separate(date, into = c("year", "month", "day")) |>
  mutate(
     prcp = prcp / 10,
     tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
     tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10
  ) # converting temperature from tenths of degrees celsius to degrees celsius, precipitation to tenths of mms to mms


ny_noaa_clean |>
  count(snow) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
  
```

The most common observed values for snowfall is 0 mm observed 1112758 times and 25 mm observed 15809 times. For most of the year in Spring, Summer, and Fall it does not snow at all in New York. It also does not snow every day in Winter. So, the most commonly observed amount of snowfall for the whole year would be 0 mm. 


```{r}
jan_july_temp =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(month %in% c("01", "07")) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

jan_july_temp |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .5) +
  facet_grid(~month) +
  labs(
    title = "New York Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature",
    color = "Location",
    caption = "data from NOAA for multiple weather stations"
  )
```

January has a lower overall average mean temperature than July. January has more variation and outliers across the years compared to July. 


```{r}
# tmax vs tmin for the full dataset 
temp_plot =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  ggplot(aes(x=tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_hex(bins=60) +
  labs(
    title = "Temperature (Max vs Min)",
    x = "Min Temperature (C)",
    y = "Max Temperature (C)"
    )

#snow distribution 
snow_dist =
  ny_noaa_clean |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  group_by(year) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = snow, y = year)) +
  geom_density_ridges(alpha=.5) +
   labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Snowfall (mm)",
    y = "Year"
)

#Two-panel plot
gridExtra::grid.arrange(temp_plot, snow_dist, ncol = 2)
```


## Problem 2

```{r}
demo_df = read_csv("~/Documents/P8105 Data Science/viz_and_eda/p8105_hw3_jv3014/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na()

accel_df = read_csv("nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names()

nhanes = inner_join(demo_df, accel_df, by = "seqn") |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
    mutate(
    sex = case_match(
      sex,
      1 ~ "Male",
      2 ~ "Female"
    ),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    education = case_match(
      education,
      1 ~ "Less than high school",
      2 ~ "High school equivalent",
      3 ~ "More than high school"
    ),
    education = factor(
      education, 
      levels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )

```


```{r}
gender_edu =
  nhanes |>
  group_by(sex, education) |>
  summarize(count. = n()) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Participant Count by Education Level and Sex")

age_edu =
  nhanes |>
  select(age, sex, education) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_density(alpha = .5) +
  facet_grid(.~education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution Across Education Categories by Sex",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Sex"
  )

gender_edu
age_edu

```

The highest concentration of participants resides in the "More than high school" tier. In contrast, fewer individuals fall into the remaining tiers, meaning trends derived from the highest education group may show more statistical stability. Within the Less than high school and High school equivalent cohorts, the age curve leans significantly toward older individuals (skewed heavily toward ages 60–80). Within the More than high school tier, the distribution slopes in the opposite direction. It features a prominent peak of younger adults (ages 20–40), demonstrating that higher education levels skew younger within this sample.


```{r}
total_activity_df = 
  nhanes |> 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, education) |>
  summarize(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(total_activity_df, aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE, method = "loess") +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity vs. Age by Education Level",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

Across all education cohorts, total movement patterns reliably degrade as individuals age.
In the Less than high school cohort, males exhibit marginally higher movement totals across middle age, but lines cross as they advance past age 60. In the High school equivalent and More than high school brackets, females maintain a higher volume of daily activity across almost all life stages compared to males.


```{r}
diurnal_df = 
  nhanes |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min"))) |>
  group_by(minute, sex, education) |>
  summarize(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(diurnal_df, aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = sex), method = "loess", span = 0.15, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 1440, by = 240),
    labels = c("Midnight", "4 AM", "8 AM", "Noon", "4 PM", "8 PM", "Midnight")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Profiles by Education Level and Sex",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Average Activity (MIMS)",
    color = "Sex"
  )
```

All groups activity drops to near zero during expected sleeping hours (11 PM to 5 AM), spikes sharply between 6 AM and 9 AM as individuals wake up, and tapers down in the late evening.

## Problem 3

This zip file contains data on rides taken on the NYC Citi Bike system. Files contain 1% of all rides with a total duration less than 4 hours in each of four months. Import, clean, and tidy these data, and describe the resulting dataset.

```{r}
library(lubridate)

jan_20 = read_csv("citibike/Jan 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "January")
jan_24 = read_csv("citibike/Jan 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "January")
jul_20 = read_csv("citibike/July 2020 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(year = 2020, month = "July")
jul_24 = read_csv("citibike/July 2024 Citi.csv.zip") |>
  mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")

data = bind_rows(jan_20, jan_24, jul_20, jul_24)

citibike =
  data |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  drop_na() |>
  filter(duration < 240)

```

The final tidied dataset contains thousands of observations representing a 1% sample of trips under 4 hours. The columns clearly document the bike type (classic vs. electric), trip timing, station endpoints, and user membership category.


```{r}
citibike |>
group_by(year, month, member_casual) |>
summarise(total_rides = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = total_rides, values_fill = 0) |>
mutate(Total = casual + member) |>
rename(Year = year, Month = month, `Casual Riders` = casual, `Citi Bike Members` = member) |>
knitr::kable(caption = "Total Number of Rides")

```

There is a substantial increase in overall ridership from 2020 to 2024. Summer ridership (July) drastically outpaces winter ridership (January) across both user types due to favorable weather conditions. Citi Bike Members consistently represent the vast majority of trips. This is especially visible during January, confirming that members rely heavily on the system for year-round, utilitarian daily commuting, while casual riders are more active during warm weather.


```{r}

citibike |>
filter(year == 2024, month == "July", !is.na(start_station_name)) |>
group_by(start_station_name) |>
summarise(Number_of_Rides = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
slice_max(order_by = Number_of_Rides, n = 5) |>
knitr::kable(caption = "Five Most Popular Citibike Starting Stations July 2024")

```



```{r}
median_duration_df <- citibike |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarise(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(median_duration_df, aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, group = interaction(year, month))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(year ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Effects of Time on Median Citi Bike Ride Durations",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)"
  ) 
```

Across all panels, the median ride duration spikes significantly on Saturdays and Sundays compared to weekdays.  July trips have a higher median duration than January trips. Colder weather in January naturally discourages lingering rides. The median ride durations are generally shorter in 2024 than in 2020.


```{r}
citibike_2024 = citibike |>
  filter(year == 2024)

ggplot(citibike_2024, aes(x = member_casual, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(month ~ rideable_type) +
  labs(
    title = "2024 Citi Bike Ride Duration Distributions",
    x = "User Membership Status",
    y = "Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    fill = "Bike Type"
  )
```

Electric bike trips show a much tighter distribution with a lower median duration than classic bikes. Because ebikes travel faster, trips are completed quicker. Casual riders have a much wider distribution spread with longer tail ends (higher variance) regardless of bike type. Members display highly predictable, compact distributions centered around shorter trip lengths (10–15 minutes). July pushes both groups to extend their classic bike rides longer, causing a rightward skew in the distribution density compared to January.
